lessons.title: How to actually learn a language
lessons.decision: What these lessons are, and what actually does the work

blocks.title: Why this comes first
blocks.text: If you skip this you'll use the rest of the course wrong. Two minutes here saves you months.

The reason adults fail at languages isn't that languages are hard. Children manage it, and they aren't smarter than you.

The reason is forgetting. You learn faster than you think and forget faster than you learn, and most study habits fight that instead of working with it.

Two things fix it, and both are boring.

1. Testing beats reviewing. Reading something again feels productive and barely works. Trying to recall it — and failing — is what makes it stick. Every prompt in this course is that, on purpose.
2. Spacing beats cramming. The best moment to review something is right when you're about to forget it. Ten minutes a day for a month beats a five-hour weekend, and it isn't close.

blocks.title: Why input matters most
blocks.text: Here's the part most apps won't tell you. Grammar is absorbed, not installed. You pick it up by understanding lots of real Spanish — podcasts, shows, conversation, YouTube — not by drilling rules.

So what is this course for?

These lessons are exposure and awareness. They give you the shape of a thing so that when it goes past you in real speech, you notice it instead of it washing over you.

The lesson makes you aware. The input makes you fluent.

Which means the honest version of the deal:

Everything here is a refresher and a set of examples. The depth comes from you — from hours of listening to native speech, and from wanting it enough to keep going back.

No app substitutes for that. This one just makes the hours count for more.

blocks.title: How to use these lessons
blocks.text:
Say every answer out loud before you check. Silent guessing barely works.

Be wrong often — that's the mechanism, not a failure.

Short and daily beats long and rare.

And go find something to listen to. The rule for picking: you should mostly understand it, and you should actually want to. Bored is worse than easy.

Start where a child starts — simple language, obvious pictures, endless repetition. That's not beneath you, it's the fastest route in.

Made for learners — the gentlest start, because they slow down and use pictures:

• Dreaming Spanish (YouTube) — graded beginner to advanced, the most recommended thing there is
• Easy Spanish (YouTube) — real street interviews, dual subtitles
• Español con Juan — slow, funny, all in Spanish
• Coffee Break Spanish or the Duolingo Spanish Podcast — short, structured, half English at first

Made for children — simple grammar, repeated constantly, and short enough to finish:

• Pocoyó — almost no dialogue, great at the very start
• Peppa Pig and Bluey dubbed in Spanish — short episodes, everyday words
• Plaza Sésamo
• Picture books and graded readers — Olly Richards' Short Stories in Spanish is built for exactly this

Made for everyone else — for when you can follow the gist:

• Something you already know well, dubbed into Spanish. Knowing the plot does the work subtitles would
• Radio Ambulante — real journalism, proper stories, genuinely worth listening to on its own
• Spanish-language shows and films from Spain, Mexico, Argentina — and the accents differ, which is worth hearing early
• Music you actually like, with the lyrics up

blocks.title: The only rule that matters
blocks.text:
Pick things you'd choose anyway. Someone who loves cooking should watch Spanish cooking channels; someone who loves football should watch Spanish football coverage.

Interest is what makes you do the hours, and the hours are what make you fluent.

lessons.title: Two languages, two ways of being
lessons.decision: Why Spanish makes you say things English lets you dodge

blocks.title: Why the difference matters
blocks.text: Spanish isn't English with different words — it's a different set of choices about what you're forced to make explicit. Knowing that up front turns the hard parts from arbitrary rules into things that make sense.

The easy news first. English and Spanish share a Latin ancestor, and a large slice of English vocabulary came in from that side of the family.

You already own thousands of Spanish words. Much of this course is claiming them, not learning them.

Now the real difference. English has one word for to be. Spanish has two, and makes you pick every single time.

Ser is what something is: concrete, settled.
Estar is how it is doing: malleable, changeable.

That's not a technicality:

Estoy aburrido — I'm bored.
Soy aburrido — I'm boring.

Same English words. One choice apart.

Spanish won't let you blur what you're experiencing with what you are.

Another:

Estoy listo — I'm ready.
Soy listo — I'm clever.

Every time you describe yourself in Spanish you answer a question English never asks: is this me, or is this just today?

blocks.title: Why it becomes part of you
blocks.text:
This is a habit of mind — not translating faster.

The grammar becomes part of who you are, because it becomes how you're able to express yourself. A Spanish speaker has spent their whole life separating essence from state, because the grammar demanded it. That's what you're picking up.

The same split happens with English for, which Spanish divides into por and para.

Gracias por la ayuda — thanks for the help. This is por: the reason, the cause, the thing that already happened.

Es para ti — it's for you. This is para: the destination, the purpose, where it's headed.

And gender. El and la aren't claims about male and female — they're noun classes, like folders.

The everyday rule is simple:
-o takes el. -a takes la.

El teléfono. La música. That'll be right most of the time.

Now watch it break.

El problema — masculine, despite the -a. Words ending -ma are usually masculine; they arrived from Greek and kept their own rules.

La mano — feminine, despite the -o. And it stays mano: la mana would sit far too close to hermana, sister.

So don't hunt for meaning in gender. Learn the pattern, learn the handful that break it, and past that native speakers simply go on what sounds right — because they've heard it ten thousand times.

That's another thing only listening gives you.

blocks.title: Why a second language gives you more
blocks.text:
A second language isn't a worse copy of your first. It hands you moves yours doesn't have.

Spanish lets you say se me cayó — it fell from me — where English forces I dropped it. One language assigns blame, the other describes an event.

Sometimes a true thing is easier to say in your second language than your first.

blocks.title: What comes next
blocks.text:
Everything from here is examples, not the whole picture. Each lesson opens with why the thing matters, then shows you the shape of it.

The depth comes from your own listening. These lessons just make sure you recognise it when it goes past.

blocks.title: Why free words matter
blocks.text: Most courses start you on phrases you can't take apart. This starts you on a rule that hands you thousands of words at once — and they're ordinary words to a Spanish speaker, so using them makes you sound normal rather than textbook.
Nation becomes nación in Spanish. The ending shifts. The word doesn't.

blocks.prompt: Say each one in Spanish out loud, then check all five.

blocks.text: You didn't learn five new words. You learned one rule and collected five. There are thousands more with that same rule.

lessons.title: Where the emphasis goes
lessons.decision: The accent tells you which syllable to hit

blocks.title: Why emphasis matters
blocks.text: English swallows the syllables it doesn't stress. Spanish doesn't — every syllable gets its full value, and exactly one gets the emphasis.
Put the emphasis in the wrong place and you're often not just accented — you're saying a different word.

One more thing before you try it. Spanish vowels are short and pure.

The letter a says ah, not ay. e says eh. i says ee. o says oh. u says oo.

Five sounds, always the same. English has around twenty and changes them constantly.

Now say this out loud before I tell you anything. Commit to a guess.

Getting it wrong right now is the catalyst — it's where the new bridges between neurons get built, so the right answer becomes automatic later. A correct guess teaches you far less.

blocks.a: The accent is an instruction: emphasise the last syllable. And notice the vowels went short — oh, eh, ah, ee, oh. No say, no shun.
Same instruction, same trap. Every vowel is short and clean, and the accent tells you where the weight lands.

blocks.text: Now one with no accent mark, so the rule has to carry you.

blocks.a:
Words ending in a vowel, -n or -s take the emphasis on the second-to-last syllable — no mark needed to say so.

And that final e gets pronounced. English drops endings; Spanish never does.
This ends in -d, so the default flips: anything ending in a consonant other than -n or -s takes the emphasis on the last syllable.

blocks.text:
That's the whole system.

Ends in a vowel, -n or -s → second-to-last syllable.
Ends in any other consonant → last syllable.
An accent mark → overrides both, always.

Spanish never leaves you guessing where the emphasis goes. English does that constantly.

blocks.title: Why gender matters
blocks.text: Gender isn't a claim about the world — la mesa doesn't mean tables are womanly. It's a filing system, and its real job is agreement: article, noun and describing word all echo each other. That echo is a lot of why Spanish sounds the way it does.
Every word ending in -ción takes la. Nothing to memorise — the ending already told you.
One rule just handed you the gender of a few thousand nouns. That's the pattern for this whole course: find the rule, skip the list.

blocks.title: Why patterns matter
blocks.text: You're not collecting words, you're building a converter. Once these are in, most English abstract nouns and adjectives have a Spanish twin you can generate on the spot instead of trying to recall.
-ty becomes -dad, and those are feminine too.
-ous becomes -oso. These describe things.
-ive becomes -ivo, and -ly becomes -mente.
Things, and words to describe them. Next you get what joins the two — and it's the choice from lesson 0.

blocks.title: Why ser matters
blocks.text: This is the identity verb, and it's concrete. Reaching for ser claims something is essentially, definingly that way. When you describe yourself with it you're saying this is who I am — so it carries more weight than English am ever does.

First, something I've been dodging. I keep saying ser, then writing es. Those look like different words. They aren't.

Spanish verbs have a base form — the one in the dictionary — and then they change shape depending on who's doing it. That changing is called conjugation.

Ser is the base form: to be. You'd never say it on its own. Its shapes:

soy — I am
eres — you are
es — he, she or it is
somos — we are
son — they are

So es is ser — just ser wearing its he/she/it clothes.

English does this too, you've just stopped noticing: be becomes am, is, are, was, were. Same trick. Spanish is only more consistent about it.

For now you need one shape: es.
Es — is. For what something fundamentally is: identity, origin, what kind of thing it is.
Notice famosa, not famoso. It's la universidad, so the describing word follows it to -a. That's the agreement from lesson 3 doing its job.
One word, and every noun and adjective you've collected just became a sentence.

blocks.title: Why estar matters
blocks.text: Estar is the verb of right now, and it's malleable. It's how Spanish speakers talk about mood, condition and place — things that could be different tomorrow. Learning to reach for it is learning to stop turning passing states into permanent claims about yourself.
Está — also is. But for where something is, or how it's doing at the moment.
Both words are is. English uses one for two jobs and never makes you notice. Spanish splits them — and the next lesson is that split.

blocks.title: Why the choice matters
blocks.text: This is the mistake English speakers make most, and it isn't cosmetic. Say soy aburrido when you meant estoy aburrido and you've announced you're boring rather than bored. The grammar makes a claim about you either way.
The working rule, and it's a good one: permanent → ser, temporary → estar. That carries you through most of what you say day to day, so lean on it.

Clearest side by side:

El hielo es frío — ice is cold. That's what ice is.
La sopa está fría — the soup is cold. It isn't supposed to be.

Same adjective. One is the nature of the thing, one is its current state.

Now the seam, so it doesn't blindside you later.

Es joven — he is young. Being young is about as temporary as things get, and it still takes ser.

Why? Because it's a category he belongs to, not a condition he's in.

So permanent-versus-temporary is the surface of something deeper: am I naming what it is, or how it's doing / where it is?

Essence or category → ser.
Condition or place → estar.

Use permanent/temporary as your everyday guide. When it feels wrong, drop to this one.

blocks.en: the conversation is important — essence or condition?
the conversation is here — which one?

blocks.title: Why this becomes a habit
blocks.text:
Every time you use one of these you make a small statement about what's essential and what's passing. That's the habit of mind — and it's the biggest single thing Spanish changes about how you describe yourself.

You'll hear this distinction hundreds of times in real speech. Now you'll notice it.

blocks.title: Why the base form matters
blocks.text: English needs two words for to prepare. Spanish folds the to into the ending. That's why the next six lessons work — the base form never changes, so once you can put something in front of it, every verb you recognise comes along.
Preparar is to prepare. The -ar does the job of the word to.
You can only recognise these so far. Six lessons from now you'll be using every one of them.

blocks.title: Why tener que matters
blocks.text: Spanish tends to have states where English is them — tengo hambre is I have hunger, not I am hungry. Obligation works the same way: you don't become obliged, you carry an obligation. Same idea, different relationship to it.
Tengo que — I have to. What follows doesn't change at all.

blocks.en: I have to visit the university

blocks.text: Learn this shape properly. Five more openings use it, and this is only the first.

blocks.title: Why deber matters
blocks.text: Tengo que is pressure from outside — circumstances say so. Debo is pressure from inside, closer to duty or conscience. Spanish separates the two; English blurs both into have to and should.
Debo — I should. Same shape you just learned.
Second opening, nothing new to learn. That's what the shape buys you.

lessons.title: Poder — being able, and saying no
lessons.decision: puedo + base form, and no in front

blocks.title: Why no matters
blocks.text: Negation is where Spanish is genuinely simpler and you should enjoy it. English rebuilds the sentence — I decide becomes I don't decide, with a helper verb out of nowhere. Spanish puts no at the front and leaves everything else alone.
Puedo — I can.
Now negate anything. No goes in front. Nothing else moves.

blocks.en: I don't have to visit the university
blocks.es: no tengo que visitar la universidad
blocks.p: noh TEN-goh keh vee-see-TAHR lah oo-nee-vehr-see-DAHD

blocks.text: One small word, and everything you've built so far just doubled.

blocks.title: Why querer matters
blocks.text: Querer is also how you say you love someone — te quiero. English has one word for love and makes it enormous; Spanish has a warm everyday one and a weightier one, and knowing which to use is a genuinely cultural skill you'll only get from listening.
Quiero — I want.

blocks.en: I want to visit the university
I want to prepare the presentation

blocks.text: Fourth opening. Still the same shape.

blocks.title: Why necesitar matters
blocks.text: This one tests whether the converter from lesson 4 is running yet. You've never been taught this word, and you should still see it coming.
Necesito — I need. Look at it: necessitate. You could almost have guessed it, and soon you'll guess right often enough to stop noticing you're doing it.

blocks.en: I need to organise the education

blocks.title: Why voy a matters
blocks.text: Spanish has a real future tense, and in everyday speech people mostly don't use it. Voy a is what you'll actually hear. So this isn't a beginner's shortcut you'll replace later — it's the thing native speakers say.
Voy a — I'm going to. Two words, same behaviour as the rest.

blocks.en: I'm going to visit the university
I'm not going to accept the situation
blocks.es: no voy a aceptar la situación
blocks.p: noh voy ah ah-sep-TAHR lah see-twah-see-OHN

blocks.text: Six openings — tengo que, debo, puedo, quiero, necesito, voy a — across every verb you recognise, with no available on any of them. Add ser and estar and you can describe things, place them, and say what you intend to do about them.

blocks.title: Why the listening comes next
blocks.text:
Every one of those sentences made you choose what's essential versus what's passing. That choice is the thing you're actually learning.

Now go and hear it. Put on something in Spanish and catch ser, estar and these six openings going past. You'll hear them within minutes — and that's where this starts turning into fluency.
